Thankfully, we sought care elsewhere before putting our dog to sleep as told the veterinary team took the time to treat our dog and ultimately helped save her life all at a reasonable price. She is alive today, and we are incredibly grateful that we got a second opinion our expenses went from $8000 at this hospital to $600 at the other vet
This experience was heartbreaking, and I hope this hospital takes a serious look at how they communicate with families during emergencies.  When someone brings in a beloved pet who is fighting for their life, they deserve to feel that the team is fighting alongside

1 star. I genuinely do not understand how this emergency vet has a 4.7 star rating after what I experienced.

My cat was attacked by a raccoon, and I brought her here because I was desperate to save her. I paid $2,375.52 upfront. I am a college student already struggling financially, so $2,375.52 is a serious amount of money to me. That can cover rent, school expenses, transportation, debt payments, or other major necessities. I still paid it because this was my cat and I wanted her alive.

After paying $2,375.52, they wanted another $3,647.57, which would have brought the total to $6,023.09. I never paid the additional $3,647.57 because I simply did not have that kind of money available.

What bothers me is that after already paying $2,375.52, I expected the immediate critical problems to be treated and my cat to at least be stabilized as much as reasonably possible before I was being presented with another massive bill.

They already knew there were air pockets associated with her injuries and knew she was in serious condition. From what was explained to me and from what I personally witnessed, I never felt that those critical problems had actually been brought under control before the conversation turned into needing another $3,647.57.

I was left wondering what exactly the $2,375.52 I had already paid accomplished if my cat was still in such critical condition that she could not even survive the ride home.

Because my cat died on the ride back home after leaving this vet. That is something I will have to live with for the rest of my life.

While I was there, I also personally saw around three or four other pets die. I understand that this is an emergency vet and they deal with animals that are already severely injured or critically ill. I am not saying that every death means the vet did something wrong. But when you are standing there watching multiple animals die, you expect to see an overwhelming level of urgency, seriousness, communication, and compassion.

Instead, during my cat’s first procedure, I saw the veterinarian laughing. I do not know what they were laughing about, and I am not claiming they were laughing at my cat, but when your animal has just been attacked and may be dying in front of you, watching the person treating her laughing during that moment is something you do not forget. I was terrified. Nothing about that situation felt funny to me.

The entire experience felt horribly transactional. This place was not sitting empty waiting for customers either. There were animals and worried owners constantly coming through. When an emergency vet is this busy and owners are being charged thousands of dollars at a time, I think it is completely reasonable to expect the medical urgency to feel at least as important as the financial urgency.

That was the biggest problem for me. I never felt like saving my cat was as urgent as getting the next payment. I understand that veterinary care costs money. I understand that no veterinarian can guarantee an animal will survive, especially after a serious attack. I was not expecting a miracle or a guarantee. What I expected after paying $2,375.52 was aggressive attention to the critical issues they had already identified, clear explanations about exactly what had been treated and what had not, and for my cat to be as stable as reasonably possible before leaving.

Instead, I paid $2,375.52 that I could barely afford, was told they wanted another $3,647.57 that I simply did not have, bringing the proposed total to $6,023.09, and then my cat died before we even made it home.

Then I look at Google and see 4.7 stars with more than 1,000 reviews, and I honestly struggle to reconcile that rating with what I personally witnessed. I cannot speak for anybody else’s experience, and I am not going to accuse anyone of something I cannot prove, but my experience was nowhere remotely close to five stars. I came here trying to save a member of my family. I left after paying $2,375.52, grieving, financially worse off than I already was, and with an empty carrier.

This information could have been shared during my initial phone call, it would have saved me the trip and unnecessary stress when I was already in panic mode trying to get help for my dog.

A female veterinarian later spoke with me, listened attentively, and was much more supportive, which I truly appreciated. However, while waiting outside afterward, I overheard her discussing with a colleague something about "it's not about age," followed by the other staff member saying, "I hate how they mention age when it's not." I couldn't be sure if this was about my dog or another dog, but conversations like this should be kept private; especially when clients are nearby. It made me uncomfortable to hear that staff speaking casually (and loudly) while eating, particularly when I was already upset about the level of care my dog received.

As professionals, the team should expect a range of behaviors from anxious or reactive dogs and handle them with patience and clear communication. The initial phone doctor could have asked more about my dog's temperament and clarified their dental capabilities upfront. Instead, I felt they gave up quickly, provided only minimal assistance (prescribing Gabapentin), and charged for the full emergency visit.

To other owners of anxious or reactive dogs: when seeking emergency care, try to ask upfront if the clinic is willing and able to accommodate your dog’s specific needs and behavior. It can help avoid unnecessary stress for everyone involved.
